title: Chapter 6 – A Crack in the Blade
html:
They leave the morning after Lin Jian's seventh birthday, with the thornback's tusks wrapped in oiled cloth on his mother's back and a story ready for anyone who asks.

The story is that they are going to sell the tusks. That part is true. A horn trader keeps a stall at the crossroads market below Willow Ford every tenth day, and he pays better than the shops in town for anything off a beast. What the story leaves out is the detour.

At the crossroads below the eastern terraces, instead of turning south toward the river and the town, his mother turns east, onto a narrow cart track that climbs into the hills. She does not explain. Lin Jian does not ask.

The track runs through bamboo. Whole valleys of it, green and gold, the stems as thick as his arm and so tall that they meet overhead and turn the road into a long, rustling tunnel. The light comes through in green bars. The wind moves the tops and the whole forest creaks and knocks like a ship at anchor. It is very beautiful and very lonely, and in two hours of walking they pass no one at all.

In the second valley they hear the iron.

It is not hammering. It is a high, sweet, uneven chiming, like temple bells hung in a wind. As they come around the shoulder of the hill, Lin Jian sees where it is coming from. The trees at the mouth of a narrow ravine are hung with metal. Bent hoes. Broken scythes. Old plowshares, cracked cooking pots, lengths of chain, horseshoes, dozens of knife blades without handles, all of it strung on wire from the branches and turning slowly in the breeze, ringing against one another. Rust has turned most of it orange. Some of it still shines.

"He says it keeps the birds off his roof," his mother says. "I think he just likes the sound."

The ravine opens into a clearing. A stream comes down one side over a series of rock ledges, and someone has built a channel off it, a wooden trough on stilts, that runs to a waterwheel on the side of a low stone building with a blackened chimney. The wheel turns slowly, creaking. Inside the building, something breathes: a deep, rhythmic whoosh, in and out, like a sleeping giant.

Bellows, Lin Jian realizes. Driven by the wheel. A water-powered forge.

The clearing is littered with the evidence of a life lived without visitors. Heaps of black slag. Stacks of charcoal under a lean-to. A garden of sorts, mostly weeds. And empty wine jars. A great many empty wine jars, piled against the wall of the house, gray with dust and green with moss, the oldest of them half buried in the earth.

A man is sitting on an upturned crate outside the forge door with his back against the stones, his eyes closed, a jar in his lap.

He is broad. Not fat; broad, like a barrel or a bull, with a chest that strains his leather apron and a neck as thick as Lin Jian's waist. His hair is gray and cropped close to his skull. His beard is long and grizzled and singed short in places, as if he has leaned too close to a fire too many times. His face has been broken at some point, the nose flattened and set badly, and the skin of his forearm is mottled with old burn scars, pink and white and shiny.

His forearm. His left one. His right sleeve is folded and pinned to his shoulder, empty.

Lin Jian looks at the man's face, and keeps looking at it.

"Hu," says his mother.

The man opens his eyes. They are a pale, ash-gray color, startling in that weathered face, and they go straight to Su Qinghe and stay there. For a moment nothing at all happens in his expression. Then something does, something complicated, and it goes away again.

"Qinghe," he says. His voice is deep and rough, as if it has not been used much lately. "It's been a long time."

"Nine years."

"Nine years." He looks at Lin Jian. "And you've brought a pup."

"My son. Lin Jian."

Old Hu looks at him a long moment. "What happened to the bow?"

"I gave it up."

"Hm." He takes a drink from the jar. Then he sets it down very carefully on the ground beside the crate, as if putting down something that might break. "You didn't walk two valleys to sell me a boar's tusk. What do you want?"

\ \ \*

His name, as it turns out, is Hu Tieshou, and he is at the ninth layer of Qi Refining.

Lin Jian feels it the moment the man looks at him: the same steady, heavy pressure he feels from his grandfather, as dense and settled as a stone at the bottom of a river. Peak of the ninth layer. And yet he lives alone in a ravine, mending hoes for farmers, and drinks.

His mother tells Lin Jian a little of it on the walk, in a voice too low for the trees to hear. Fifteen years ago, on an island in the Eastern Sea, she was a rogue cultivator taking whatever work came, and Hu Tieshou was a master weapon-smith with a workshop of his own and a reputation that reached across the sea. Then one night his workshop burned. She was passing. She pulled him out. He had been bleeding for an hour and there were men waiting outside the door.

"What men?" Lin Jian asks.

"Men who wanted him dead." She shakes her head. "He owes me his life. He has never said so, and I have never asked him to. Neither of us talks about that night." She looks down at him. "So don't ask."

He does not ask.

Hu, it turns out, does not ask very much either. He lets them sit on two more crates in the shade of the forge, and he listens while Su Qinghe explains, in very few words, that her son likes to make things and is better at it than he should be, and needs someone to teach his hands.

When she has finished, Hu looks at Lin Jian for a long, uncomfortable moment.

"How old?"

"Seven," says Lin Jian.

"Root?"

"Pseudo. All five."

Hu grunts. "Can't teach roots. Wouldn't if I could." He gets up from his crate, a little unsteadily, and goes into the forge. When he comes back he is carrying something wrapped in a greasy rag. He drops it in Lin Jian's lap.

"Tell me what's wrong with that."

Lin Jian unwraps it.

It is a dagger. Or it was. A slim blade about as long as his forearm, dark gray with a faint bluish sheen, snapped clean in two about a third of the way up from the hilt. The steel has a strange feel to it, faintly cool, faintly alive, the way the guards' arm-guards feel but stronger.

"Spirit iron," Hu says. "A hunter brought it to me last month. He'd hit a wolf on the shoulder bone with it, and it broke. He wants to know if I can mend it. He wants to know if it was his fault." He sits down again. "You tell me."

Lin Jian turns the two pieces over in his hands.

In his first life, he spent eleven years studying exactly this. Not spirit iron. Steel, titanium, superalloys, the metal in turbine blades and bridge cables and aircraft landing gear. Why they bent and why they broke. How you could tell, from the broken face of a piece of metal, the whole history of how it failed.

He does not need to scan it. He only needs to look.

He holds the broken face up to the light.

"The inside is like sugar," he says slowly. He keeps his words simple. He chooses them as if he is finding them for the first time. "Big grains. Shiny. It should be smooth, like this part near the edge." He points. "So the middle got too hot. When you made it."

Hu says nothing.

"And there are lines on the broken part. Like ripples on sand, when the water goes out. They all point back to here." He touches a spot on the fracture face near the spine of the blade, a tiny dark speck no bigger than a grain of rice. "That's where it started. There's a dirty bit in the metal. Something that isn't iron. The crack started there and ran out from it."

Hu's face does not change. But he has stopped drinking.

"And the edge has tiny cracks in it, all along," Lin Jian says. "Like a cup that's been put in cold water while it's hot. So it was cooled too fast. In cold water." He looks up. "You should cool it in oil. Oil is slower."

Silence.

The bellows breathe in the forge. The metal in the trees chimes.

"How," says Old Hu at last, very quietly, "do you know the inside was too hot?"

Lin Jian looks at him. "I looked at it."

"Who taught you?"

"Nobody. I just looked at it."

Hu Tieshou stares at him. Then he takes the two halves of the dagger out of Lin Jian's hands and holds the broken face up to the light himself, and peers at it, and his lips move. Lin Jian sees him find the dark speck near the spine, and stop.

"I was drunk," Hu says, to the dagger. "When I forged it. I left it in the coals while I went for another jar. Twenty minutes. Maybe thirty." He turns it, looking at the edge. "And the hunter wanted it fast, so I quenched it in the stream. And the speck." He touches it with the tip of a scarred finger. "Slag. I never saw it. Forty years of forging, and I never saw it."

He sets the pieces down on his knee and looks at Lin Jian again, and this time his pale eyes do not move away.

"Qinghe," he says, without looking at her. "What is this boy?"

"My son," says Su Qinghe evenly.

"That's not what I asked."

"It's all the answer I have."

Hu looks at her then. Something passes between them that Lin Jian cannot read.

"I made things that killed people," Hu says suddenly. He says it to the dagger. "The last things I made. For people who used them for something I can't forget. So I came here, and I mend hoes, and I don't make weapons, and I drink." He picks up the jar and puts it down again without drinking. "What do you want me to make him? A sword? A spear?"

"I want you to teach him," Su Qinghe says. "Whatever his hands want to learn. And I want you to come to Green Pine Hill and live there and let everyone see that you teach him." She meets his eyes. "My son is going to make things, Hu. People are going to wonder how a seven-year-old boy with a pseudo-root makes them. When they wonder, I want them to look at you."

Old Hu is silent for a long time.

"A wall," he says at last.

"A teacher," says Su Qinghe. "And a wall."

Hu looks at Lin Jian. "What do you want, boy? A teacher, or a wall?"

Lin Jian thinks about it honestly. "Both," he says.

Something happens to Old Hu's broken face that might be the beginning of a smile. It does not get very far.

\ \ \*

They talk terms. Or rather, his mother talks terms, and Hu grunts.

He will come to Green Pine Hill as a guest elder of the Lin Clan, for one year. He will have a room and a forge and his food and his wine. He will mend the family's tools. He will teach Lin Jian, and only Lin Jian, whatever Lin Jian's hands want to learn.

"And if at the end of the year I don't like it," Hu says, "I come back here."

"Agreed."

"And don't call me Elder. I'm not anybody's elder. Old Hu is fine."

"Agreed."

Then he is quiet for a moment, scratching his singed beard.

"Green Pine Hill," he says. "That's the Lin family. Old Patriarch at the ninth layer, a hundred and some, no Foundation. Neighbor on Red Ridge is a Zhao with a Foundation and a second-grade vein." He looks at Su Qinghe sidelong. "I hear things, even out here. The farmers talk while I fix their plows. They say the Zhao have been leaning on your hill for twenty years, and the old man is running out of time, and when he goes the Zhao will have the whole valley by the next harvest."

"The farmers talk too much."

"Farmers are usually right about weather and neighbors." Hu picks up his jar, looks into it, and puts it down again. "You're not asking me to come and teach a boy to make hoes, Qinghe. You're asking me to come and live on a hill that's going to be in a war."

"I'm asking you to teach my son."

"I don't fight wars anymore."

"Then don't," says Su Qinghe. "Mend hoes. Drink. Teach him. Nobody on Green Pine Hill will ask you to pick up a weapon." She pauses. "I won't ask you either."

Hu looks at her for a long time. Then he looks at the hanging iron at the mouth of the ravine, turning slowly in the wind, chiming.

"You never did ask," he says at last, half to himself. "Fifteen years, and you never once asked me for anything." He sighs, a long rasping breath that seems to come up from somewhere under his ribs. "Fine."

He turns to Lin Jian. "And you," he says. "One rule. If you ever lie to me, boy, I'll know. And I'll go." He leans forward. "Understand?"

"Yes."

"Good."

He holds out his hand. His left hand, since he has no other. Lin Jian, who has watched the guards in the gate yard seal their wagers, knows what it means: among rogue cultivators, a bargain is closed with the left hand, the hand without a weapon in it. He puts out his own left hand, and Old Hu's enormous, scarred, calloused palm closes around it.

The scan happens before he can stop it.

He has not meant to. He has not focused. But he is touching a man who has spent forty years soaking in the Qi of his forge and his metals, and some part of him that has been reaching for new things all day reaches for this one too. The blue line sweeps. He feels the cold go out of him, through his palm, into Hu's.

```
[Scan: Human (Male, ~64 years)]
Cultivation: Qi Refining, Layer 9 (peak)
Body: Extensive thermal scarring. Right arm severed at shoulder (approx. 15 years ago).

[Anomaly Detected]
Foreign energy residue in right shoulder channels.
Type: Blood-attribute Qi. Corrosive. Dormant.
Structure: Woven into host's own Qi signature (grafted pattern).
Note: Grafted pattern mimics host Qi. Undetectable by Qi-based perception.
Detected by material analysis only.
Effect: Slow degradation of shoulder and chest channels.
Origin: Deliberately inflicted.

Creation Energy +2 (52 / 100)
```

Lin Jian does not let go of the hand. He does not let his face change. It takes every bit of discipline he has.

But Old Hu's hand has gone very still in his.

Slowly, the old smith looks down at their joined hands. Then at Lin Jian's face. His pale eyes narrow, very slightly, the way Uncle Mao's narrowed the day he saw Lin Jian on the storehouse roof.

He lets go.

"Well," he says. "That's that." He gets up and goes into the forge without another word, and they hear him banging about inside, and the bellows go on breathing.

His mother looks at Lin Jian. Lin Jian looks at the ground.

\ \ \*

While his mother waits in the shade and Hu packs, Lin Jian walks among the trees at the mouth of the ravine, looking up at the hanging iron, and touching what he can reach.

Most of it is ordinary metal, rusted, worthless. But not all. A curved offcut of something dark and smooth that hums under his fingers. A hook made from a sliver of the same bluish spirit iron as the dagger. A lump of slag the size of his fist that turns out, when he scans it, to be full of tiny bright flecks of some metal the panel cannot name.

```
[Scan: Spirit Iron Offcut] Creation Energy +3
[Scan: Slag (Spirit-Metal Inclusions)] Creation Energy +2
[Scan: Hook (Yellow Grade Fragment)] Creation Energy +2

Creation Energy: 59 / 100
```

Old Hu comes out of the forge with a sack over his shoulder and finds him standing under the trees.

"Like my orchard?" he asks.

"What's this?" Lin Jian holds up the hook.

Hu takes it from him and turns it over. "Piece of a spirit-iron fishhook I made for a fisherman on the coast. Yellow grade. Holds an edge forever and the fish can't throw it." He hangs it back on its wire. "Mortal grade is what a smith makes with fire and hammer and a little spirit copper, for men who don't cultivate. Yellow grade is what a smith makes when he cultivates himself, and puts some of his own Qi into the metal while it's soft. For people like you and me. Most smiths in this county can't make Yellow grade. The ones who can charge a month's rice for a fishhook." He looks up at the hanging iron. "Profound grade, you need a Foundation cultivator's fire, or a furnace with a formation in it. Something that burns hot enough to melt the spirit out of a metal and put it back in the shape you want."

Lin Jian thinks about that. Mortal grade: fire and hammer. Yellow: fire, hammer and the smith's own Qi. Profound: a heat no Qi Refining body can make on its own. It is not so different from what he knows. A blacksmith's forge, an electric furnace, a vacuum arc. Each step up the ladder of materials in his first life was a step up the ladder of temperatures, and each one cost more energy than the last.

"Have you made Profound grade?"

Old Hu does not answer for a moment. The iron chimes in the wind.

"Once or twice," he says. And then, quite gently, "Don't ask about that either."

He follows Hu back into the forge while the old smith finishes packing, because he cannot help it.

It is dark inside, and hot, and it smells of coal smoke and scorched leather and hot metal. The waterwheel's shaft comes in through the wall and turns a crank that works a pair of bellows as big as a cow, and every few heartbeats they heave and sigh and the coals in the hearth flare from red to orange. Tools hang on the walls in rows: tongs, punches, swages, chisels, hammers from the size of his fist to the size of his head. Every one of them has a handle worn smooth and dark by a hand.

A left hand. Lin Jian sees it as soon as he looks. Every handle is worn on the side a left hand would grip. And on the anvil, a heavy iron block with a horn at one end, there is a curious thing: a clamp bolted to the side, with a lever that a foot can work, to hold hot metal still while a man with one arm strikes it.

He built it himself, Lin Jian thinks. He lost his arm and learned to forge all over again, with the wrong hand, and built every tool he needed to do it.

"Stop staring at my anvil," says Old Hu, without turning round. "It's shy."

\ \ \*

The horn trader at the crossroads pays twenty-two low-grade spirit stones for the tusks, after half an hour of haggling that Su Qinghe conducts with the cheerful ferocity of a woman who has been cheated by horn traders before. Twenty-two stones. Lin Jian does the conversion in his head. A Willow Ford laborer earns about one stone a month. Fourth Uncle's guards get two. The clan's whole autumn tribute is three hundred. A boar that tried to kill him is worth nearly a year of a farmer's work.

He thinks about that, and about the hanging iron in Old Hu's trees, for most of the walk home.

They walk back through the bamboo as the sun goes down, the three of them in single file, Old Hu at the back with his sack and a jar of wine he has not opened. At the edge of the last valley he stops, and Lin Jian, glancing back, sees him rub his right shoulder with his left hand, slowly, in small hard circles, the way his father rubs his own left shoulder at night.

His mother sees it too. She drops back to walk beside him.

"Does it still hurt?"

"Every day." Hu says it without self-pity, as if he is reporting the weather. "Worse every year. It spreads. Last winter it got into my chest. Some mornings I cough." He shrugs his one shoulder. "I've seen three healers. A temple doctor on the coast. A Sect alchemist in the islands who charged me forty stones to tell me nothing. And the last one, a Nascent Soul elder of the Coral Tide Sect, who looked at it as a favor to an old customer." He snorts. "A Nascent Soul elder. Do you know what that's like, Qinghe? His spiritual sense went through me like a cold wind. Through every channel. Every bone. I could feel him counting my teeth from the inside."

"And?"

"And he found nothing." Hu's voice is flat. "Nothing but my own Qi. He said it was a furnace burn that had turned inward. A smith's sickness. Too many years breathing hot metal. He said it would kill me slowly and there was nothing anyone could do, and he was very sorry, and he had a meeting." He walks on for a while. "I knew he was wrong. I knew what it was the night it happened. But if a Nascent Soul elder can't see it, it isn't there. That's how the world works, isn't it?"

Su Qinghe says nothing.

Ahead of them, on the darkening road, Lin Jian keeps walking and does not look back.

Blood-attribute Qi, he thinks. Woven into his own signature. Undetectable by Qi-based perception. A Nascent Soul elder, a cultivator four great realms above anyone on Green Pine Hill, felt for the wound with his own spiritual sense and found only Hu's own Qi, wearing a disguise. Every cultivator in this world looks at the world through Qi. Whoever did this to Hu knew that.

The interface does not look through Qi. It looks at what things are made of.

He remembers Uncle Mao's voice from a lesson on the five elements, years ago, when Lin Hu had asked if there were any more.

There are other kinds of Qi, the old man had said. Lightning. Ice. Wind. And there is blood. He had not raised his voice, but every child in the courtyard had gone quiet. Blood Qi comes from one place only. The demonic path. If you ever meet a man whose Qi smells of iron and salt, children, you run, and you do not stop running until you are home.

Behind him on the darkening road, the one-armed smith walks in silence, and his Qi is quiet and steady and smells of nothing but charcoal and wine.

And somewhere under it, where no cultivator will ever find it, something red is slowly eating him alive.
